issues.explanation: Occupation 'Student' is implausible for age 59 under the validation rules (Student is implausible if age > 40).

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Mele is an 80-year-old Tongan American woman who has spent most of her adult life working as a welder in a small fabrication shop, a job she still takes pride in keeping despite her age. She came to treatment after years of physical abuse by her husband, abuse that had become woven into the ordinary spaces of her life. The worst incidents happened at home at night, often after she had already changed for bed and believed the day was over. She described lying in the dark listening for the shift in his breathing or the sound of his footsteps in the hallway, knowing from experience how quickly a quiet evening could turn. More than once she was hit hard enough that afterward she felt stunned by her own body, as if it had ceased to belong to her and become something frail and easily broken.

In the months and years that followed, Mele had come to believe that what happened had permanently damaged her. She spoke less about bruises than about a deeper conviction that her body had been altered for good, that it was now unreliable and could fail her without warning. When she felt soreness, fatigue, or the ordinary stiffness of age, she did not experience those sensations as neutral. She took them as proof that the abuse had left lasting harm and that she could no longer trust her own body to protect or steady her. What frightened her almost as much was the sense that her emotional life had gone flat. She told the therapist she would never feel normal emotions again, as though some part of her capacity for ease or warmth had been beaten out of her. Because she was certain she was physically vulnerable and internally changed, she stayed on guard even in her own house, unable to believe that rest was safe.

That sense of danger now shapes her nights. She has trouble falling asleep, and when she does sleep it is light and fractured. She wakes abruptly and sits up to check whether she is safe, listening toward the bedroom door and the rooms beyond it before she can even orient herself fully. She described scanning the house in the dark, alert to small noises that her husband might not even notice. At home she remains tense in a way that feels automatic, as if her body has learned that walls and locks do not mean protection. Working in the welding shop gives her some structure, but even there the rhythm of metal striking metal can leave her body braced before she has time to think. By the time she returns home, she is already anticipating another night of broken sleep.

Those nights have gradually reinforced what she believes about herself. Each time she wakes suddenly to check the house, Mele reads her own reaction as further evidence that her body is no longer trustworthy. She notices her heart racing, the stiffness in her shoulders, the inability to settle again, and concludes that something inside her has been permanently damaged. The fact that she cannot sleep through the night, even in her own bed, seems to prove to her that she will never feel normal again. She has begun to speak of her body almost as if it were a separate thing that betrays her, staying vigilant when she wants rest and flooding her with alarm when she wants calm.

That belief, in turn, keeps the threat close. Because she is convinced she is physically vulnerable, she checks and rechecks her safety after waking, and because she believes her emotions will never return to normal, she does not expect comfort or relief to come. Her own home feels like a place where she must remain prepared. She sleeps lightly, wakes alert, and listens for danger; by morning she feels worn down but not reassured. The cycle has narrowed her life. After long shifts welding, she used to come home and sit with her husband in the evening or speak with relatives by phone. Now she mostly endures the hours before bed, already dreading the night.

She sought help only recently, after realizing that even on quieter nights she was still jolting awake to make sure she was safe. What finally brought her in was not one new assault but the fear that this watchfulness had become permanent, that her body and feelings had been changed beyond repair. She says she wants sleep, but what she is really asking is whether it is still possible to feel at home in herself again.
